On a quiet Monday morning, a teacher at Amban Elementary School in South Cotabato, Philippines, asks her grade 1 students a simple but powerful question: "What color is your feeling today — and what made it that color?" Small hands shoot up. Six-year-olds reach not just for crayons, but for words to describe their inner worlds.
This is social-emotional learning (SEL) in action — not an abstract concept buried in a policy document, but a living practice woven into an ordinary school day. Teachers had long been practicing SEL without necessarily calling it by name; training helped them recognize and apply these practices with greater intention. The change is visible: teachers now adjust instruction to learners' needs and deliberately nurture curiosity, confidence, and belonging — which, among the school's predominantly Indigenous Peoples students, has translated into greater participation and engagement in class.
Teachers are the single most powerful school-based factor in determining whether children learn and thrive, and acquire the skills they will need later for productive jobs, and for life. Research in the United States shows that moving from a low-performing to a high-performing teacher can accelerate student learning by months — sometimes years. In Pakistan, replacing a bottom-five-percent teacher with an average one could add up to US$250,000 in lifetime earnings per classroom. Investing in teachers delivers the highest returns in education.
The teachers from Amban Elementary School are among the beneficiaries of the ongoing Teacher Effectiveness and Competencies Enhancement Project (TEACEP) administered by the Department of Education (DepEd) and supported by the World Bank. TEACEP offers a model of what comprehensive, system-level support for teachers can look like.
Professional Development That Actually Works
How do we help teachers become more effective? The answer lies in sustained, meaningful professional development — not the one-off training workshop that fades from memory, but the kind of deep, ongoing support that sticks.
Effective programs are rooted in real classroom practice, grounded in subject content, and designed to be continuous and collaborative. Coaching is especially powerful: it gives teachers space to try new approaches, reflect on what worked, and keep improving. Professional Learning Communities take this further by creating spaces where teachers learn with and from each other. Kenya's Tusome program, which brings all these elements together, achieved reading gains in early grades equivalent to 3.5 to 5 years of learning.
Why Even Good Programs Often Stall
Here is an uncomfortable truth: even the best teacher development programs can fail when they are scaled up. Many initiatives work well as small pilots, but struggle when expanded across an entire school system — not because the ideas are wrong, but because the system around them is not designed to sustain them.
Teachers cannot thrive in weak systems. Without the right structures — clear career pathways, manageable workloads, and institutionalized support — even the most motivated teachers burn out, and the most well-designed programs quietly fade away.
Building a System for Lasting Change
The Philippines' TEACEP program has taken this challenge seriously. By pairing investments in teacher development with structural reforms to the systems in which teachers work, it has sought to create the conditions where good teaching can not only take root but also endure. The results, still unfolding, offer three important lessons for what it takes to build a profession — not just a workforce.
First, an expanded career progression system has replaced a previously opaque promotion process with a clear, merit- and competency-based pathway. During a joint visit by DepEd and the World Bank in March 2026, teachers and school leaders described it as a genuine turning point. With the right encouragement at the school level, one participant said, the process felt "smooth" and truly supportive of their goals.
Second, reforms to reduce the administrative workload have freed up time for what matters most: teaching. Teachers reported that administrative tasks are increasingly being handled by non-teaching staff, and a dedicated two-hour period is now being used for school-based professional development and home visits. School heads noted that the policy has "significantly helped teachers manage their instructional responsibilities" and given them "more time to focus on instruction."
Third, Professional Learning Communities have built a culture of shared growth, replacing isolated struggle with collective purpose. Picture a group of teachers gathered after school, exchanging lesson plans and talking through what worked — and what did not — that week. Through these exchanges, teachers gain fresh ideas and a sense of camaraderie that transforms professional development from a solitary task into a shared journey.
The work is far from finished. Schools in multigrade settings, Indigenous Peoples Education communities, and remote locations still face significant constraints, particularly where non-teaching staff are scarce. These contexts will need targeted attention as the reforms continue to mature. In many ways, how the system responds to its hardest-to-reach communities will define the lasting impact of the entire reform effort.
Lessons Worth Sharing
The early experience from the Philippines carries a message that travels well beyond its borders: empowering teachers is a system issue, not just a training problem. Workshops, coaching, and mentoring all matter — but none of them will stick without an ecosystem of enabling conditions: career incentives that reward growth, workload policies that protect instructional time, and institutional structures that outlast any single project or political cycle.
When those conditions are in place, teachers do not just survive the classroom — they flourish in it. And when teachers flourish, students bloom.
